D. THE CARVING — CORRECT TOOLS, CORRECT ORDER

Spokeshave — fairs the rough-sawn ogee curve. Both hands on the handles, pulled toward him, cutting on the pull, lifting a thin ribbon shaving out of the tool's mouth.

1. SETTING IN. A small carving gouge held VERTICALLY, its sweep matched to the drawn curve. He taps the handle with a wooden mallet — the edge sinks straight down along the pencil line, severing the fibres. Lift, rotate to follow the next curve, tap again. The outline is incised as a chain of overlapping stab cuts.

2. GROUNDING OUT. A flatter gouge held at a low angle, bevel down, cutting horizontally INTO the stabbed outline from the waste side. Chips release cleanly at the stab line and lift away. The background drops; the leaf stands proud.

3. MODELLING. A small skew chisel rolls the leaf's outer edge over into a curl; a shallow gouge hollows the centre of the lobe. The flat shape becomes a three-dimensional form.

4. VEINING. The V-parting tool cuts fine lines radiating down the leaf, following its curve. Thin twisted shavings.

5. CLEANING. A curved riffler file works into the tight recesses between the curls where no blade fits, cutting on the push, leaving fine dust.

MECHANICAL RULES:

The work is held in the bench vise or braced against a stop — it never slides freely.

The mallet strikes BEFORE the edge sinks. The edge sinks BEFORE the chip releases. Never the reverse.

Grounding cuts always run INTO a stabbed line, never away from it.

Every cut lifts a real shaving or chip that falls; they accumulate on the bench.

The relief deepens over successive passes, never in one stroke.

He blows dust from the recess and brushes the surface with his hand between stages.

Practised, economical, absorbed hands. No flourish, no sparks, no flying debris, no theatrical exertion.
